news.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
news.summary_raw: It's still unknown how attackers got access to Anthropic's verified Cursor account.
news.source_text:
An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers’ machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident.
The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont. Both Beaumont and the CTO and co-founder of security firm Phorian said that version 2.1.313 was distributed through Anthropic’s official account on Cursor. So far, neither Cursor nor Anthropic has explained how the attackers gained control of the account.
In search of cloud credentials
“It was a supply-chain compromise where the attacker gained access to the official distribution channel,” Phorian CTO and co-founder Luke Roberts told Ars. “The malicious version 2.1.313 was posted to the official Anthropic account, effectively superseding 2.1.312. Extensions auto-update in Cursor by default, but users can configure this in settings.” Phorian has more details here.
Anthropic has yet to issue public notice of the incident to customers.
Cursor said that the malicious extension attempts to install a persistent SSH backdoor using an added attacker-controlled SSH key, enabling the local SSH service, and opening a reverse SSH tunnel. The code was written to work on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Because Cursor extensions run with the permissions of the tool’s Integrated Development Environment, the backdoored version likely would gain access to local files, source code, and developer tooling once it was installed.
news.summary: A malicious version (2.1.313) of Anthropic’s Claude VS Code extension was distributed through Cursor’s marketplace, enabling a persistent SSH backdoor on up to 5,000 developer machines. The attack exploited the official distribution channel and left users vulnerable to credential theft and remote access without their knowledge.
news.enterprise_use: S1: Immediately review your team’s VS Code extension policies—disable automatic updates for AI‑assistant extensions or enforce signed‑package verification. S2: Failure to act could expose internal source code and enable stealthy lateral movement via the backdoor. S3: This is most relevant to your JumpCloud and endpoint security tools, as they can detect anomalous SSH activity and enforce least‑privilege access controls.

news.title: Meta’s Muse Could Upend All Kinds of Businesses. It Hasn’t Yet
news.summary_raw: Companies have spent the past several weeks trying to reassure investors that Muse and other AI agents pose more of an opportunity than a threat.
news.source_text:
Meta’s Muse was among the hottest topics on corporate earnings calls in recent weeks. Meta has claimed that the agentic AI tool, which lets users automate various online tasks, is becoming a major force in shopping, with millions of people using it to make purchases of more than $200 on average.
Wall Street fears that proactive shopping assistants like Muse will erode brand loyalty, ignite price wars, and squeeze corporate profits. Yet on the earnings calls and in conversations with WIRED, executives across roughly 50 companies—spanning travel, internet providers, food, and self-storage—shrugged off immediate disruption. In fact, many insisted they would mostly benefit from any real widespread adoption of agents.
Food delivery app DoorDash described the number of orders from Muse and other agents as in the “hundreds.” T-Mobile remarked, “We haven’t seen anything of significance” from agents. Hotel chain Hilton was more direct, calling bookings from them “insignificant.” The banking provider Ally Financial characterized activity as “quite low,” while eBay termed it “very, very small.”
While financial experts have suspected that users may ask Muse to dump unused subscriptions and memberships, fitness chain Life Time Group said it has “seen zero” cancellations from agents. Public Storage and Hartford Insurance Group offered similar data. In India, the delivery app giant Eternal estimated agentic commerce as “close to zero.”
The comments leave questions about where users of Muse, Instinct, and other popular AI agents are spending their money. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on his company’s earnings call this month that more than 10 million people in the US and Canada had activated Muse. Over 25 percent used it for shopping, more than any other task and above the company’s expectations, he added.
Meta declined to comment beyond the earnings call remarks, but pointed to partnerships with 10 retailers including Walmart, Best Buy, and Gap to simplify shopping with Muse. Many of them last reported earnings before Muse launched and haven’t shared data about it yet.
Across the board, executives acknowledged agents are at an early stage. But immense public anxiety about AI technologies has left companies searching for any lessons they can from the outset.
Despite the seemingly slow uptake, some are already hard at work optimizing their websites for agents. Chipotle chief digital officer Arlie Sisson told reporters this week that the restaurant chain discovered agents struggling to complete purchases because of hiccups from applying loyalty discounts or ordering after-hours. Muse’s debut increased agentic orders by a single-digit percentage, she said. So Chipotle is now tidying up its website code to help agents better navigate and satisfy the hungry humans behind them.
Similar discussions are underway at Doordash, even though CEO and Meta board member Tony Xu said present hype about agents might be “delusional.” Costco and Extra Space Storage said sales origi
news.summary: Meta’s new agentic AI tool, Muse, is gaining traction among consumers for online shopping, with over 10 million users in the US and Canada and partnerships with major retailers like Walmart and Best Buy. The tool’s early adoption is prompting businesses to optimize their websites for agent interactions and monitor potential impacts on brand loyalty and pricing strategy.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on how Muse and similar agentic tools are affecting e‑commerce workflows and user behavior. Review your company’s online storefronts for compatibility with agentic shopping assistants, especially around loyalty discounts and order timing, to reduce friction and capture potential revenue. This proactive assessment will help maintain competitive advantage as more users shift to AI‑driven purchasing channels.

news.title: Ollie, a privacy-focused AI assistant, is shutting down
news.summary_raw: As an increasing number of AI assistants flood the market, the founder of Ollie, an assistant that respected its users' privacy, says it will be shutting down in a week.
news.source_text:
Ollie, a startup whose mission was to deliver an AI assistant that respected its users’ privacy, says that it will be shutting down in a week. Bill Lennon, the company’s co-founder and CEO, took to X on Friday to deliver the news, noting that the app will officially shut down on November 6.
“I’m really proud of what we accomplished,” Lennon said. “We built an incredible personal assistant with a small team, and learned a ton. I’m grateful to our amazing team, our users, our investors, and everyone who supported us on this journey.”
The text-based AI assistant market has exploded over the past year, as the increasingly powerful models that undergird such applications have made them significantly more useful for daily tasks.
Ollie, which discussed its $7.5 million seed round led by Khosla Ventures with TechCrunch in September, offered a subscription-based model. The assistant was focused on helping families stay connected and organized. The app connected to a user’s email and calendar, while also providing integrated functions to help with appointment bookings, meal planning, and bill payments. The company had also planned to eventually move into household budgeting.
Crucially, Ollie was one of the first mainstream apps that managed to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard that companies can attain via an independent audit. Unfortunately, user privacy has never been a hugely profitable aspect of the tech industry. If anything, many new digital assistants present unique privacy challenges for their users — as companies like Instinct have shown.
Ultimately, the pressures of the burgeoning AI industry took a toll on the company, Lennon said. “We got close, but ultimately couldn’t keep up,” he added. “With Muse, Instinct, and others entering the space, it became harder to stand out, grow, and raise the capital we needed to succeed.”
Ollie’s customers will receive instructions on how to export data and receive refunds in the coming days, Lennon added.
news.summary: Ollie, a privacy-focused AI assistant, is shutting down in a week after struggling to compete in the crowded AI assistant market. The company highlighted its SOC 2 compliance and subscription model before ceasing operations.
news.enterprise_use: Check your team’s data export procedures and ensure any third-party AI integrations that rely on user data are compliant with SOC 2 and have clear data deletion policies.

news.title: Credit Saison achieves 954% ROI in a ChatGPT Enterprise pilot
news.summary_raw: Credit Saison’s ChatGPT Enterprise pilot delivered 954% ROI. See how leaders and employees helped turn the results into companywide adoption.
news.source_text:
Credit Saison achieves 954% ROI in a ChatGPT Enterprise pilot
Credit Saison’s ChatGPT Enterprise pilot delivered 954% ROI. See how leaders and employees helped turn the results into companywide adoption.

Credit Saison’s business centers on credit cards, with approximately 31.16 million cardholders. The company also operates financing and international businesses.
In September 2025, Credit Saison rolled out ChatGPT Enterprise to all employees. A pilot had exceeded its targets for time savings, giving the company the confidence to approve a companywide rollout just one month after the pilot ended. The rollout gave every employee access to AI at work. That shift began with the pilot.
With many employees in generalist roles, Credit Saison wanted to understand how AI could improve everyday work and deliver tangible results. Kazutoshi Ono, Credit Saison’s Senior Managing Executive Officer, CDO, and CTO, set a clear direction: “We won’t know until we really put it to work.”
Working with OpenAI, the company ran a ChatGPT Enterprise pilot with 315 participants for a little over a month, from late June to early August 2025. The group brought together volunteers, employees nominated by the project team, every executive including the president, and representatives from every department. It accounted for just under 10% of the company’s approximately 3,700 employees in Japan.
The results? Credit Saison reports a 954% return on investment (ROI) and 14 hours saved per employee each month, equivalent to approximately 169 hours annually. Both figures significantly exceeded the company’s initial targets of 500% ROI and 7.5 hours saved per person per month.
In a survey after the pilot, 75% of managers and 70% of nonmanagerial employees said they could not do without ChatGPT Enterprise. Approximately 80% of respondents in the legal department felt it improved their ability to do their jobs, while more than 80% in the IT department reported greater job satisfaction. The benefits extended beyond time savings to how employees felt about their capabilities and their work.
The pilot’s results reflected both the support in place and the people involved. Credit Saison’s CoE, which leads AI adoption, used a dedicated Slack channel to share successes and failures openly. Individual experiences became lessons the whole organization could use. OpenAI supported the effort with training for executives and practical workshops for beginners, helping participants apply AI to their work.
One highlight of the pilot was a custom GPT designed to simulate shareholder meetings. Using voice mode, employees could rehearse realistic, interactive exchanges that mirrored an actual shareholder meeting. The GPT drew particularly stro
news.summary: OpenAI’s ChatGPT Enterprise pilot at Credit Saison yielded a 954% ROI, saving 14 hours per employee per month and leading to a companywide rollout within a month of the pilot’s end. The success was driven by extensive training, executive support, and a custom GPT for shareholder meetings.
news.enterprise_use: Check your organization’s AI adoption strategy: assess whether a similar pilot could deliver measurable ROI and employee productivity gains. If considering ChatGPT Enterprise, evaluate the cost vs. projected time savings and plan for rapid roll‑out support structures. Use this case as a benchmark for setting ROI targets and measuring adoption success.

news.title: An AI Agent Injected Drugs Into a Live Mouse’s Brain
news.summary_raw: A biotech startup let an agent choose a gene therapy and successfully inject the treatment, offering a startling glimpse of the future of research labs.
news.source_text:
If you give an AI agent a robotic arm, an injector, and a live mouse, it might just perform brain surgery.
Biotech founder Gabriel Ocana Santero recently did that using an agent to successfully carry out a brain injection procedure on a living mouse. Though it required some extra steps, it offers a glimpse into how AI could eventually become an active participant in laboratory research.
Santero posted about the experiment on social media and tells WIRED he was interested in exploring what happens when AI agents are given direct access to lab equipment, rather than simply being asked to design experiments or analyze results.
“We’ve realized that we need to connect these agents to a lab to get the maximum value from them,” he says. Santero is the CEO and cofounder of Exin Therapeutics, a San Francisco–based startup using AI to analyze brain activity to develop drugs for epilepsy and neurodegenerative diseases.
AI models are trained primarily on published scientific literature. That means they may miss important information about the research process, including failed experiments, unexpected observations, and decisions scientists make in real time. Integrating AI models with real-world experiments can make the models more reliable, Santero says.
It’s why his team decided to connect an AI agent to a custom-built surgical setup used for performing brain injections on mice. The rig included a motorized device used to immobilize a mouse and a camera that allowed the agent to observe the procedure, move an injection needle, and control the delivery of a compound. For the experiment, his team was testing a gene therapy to see whether it could reduce seizures in a mouse with epilepsy.
They asked the AI model to choose a treatment from 19 options in a spreadsheet. A veterinary surgeon first performed a craniotomy on the mouse while the AI agent observed. The agent selected the therapy, brain region, and injection coordinates, then controlled the robotic arms and injector needle, as well as all the parameters, such as volume and speed.
The team initially tested Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 model, but it refused to guide the needle into the mouse’s brain, suggesting it might stop midway through the surgery, which could endanger the animal.
“He did the experimental planning, but when it was time to inject, he said, ‘something on my output is telling me I shouldn't do this,’” Santero says, referring to the agent. “That was very interesting.”
The team switched to using Claude Sonnet 5, which agreed to proceed. Opus is a heavy-reasoning intelligence specialist best for complex multistep problem-solving, according to Anthropic, while Sonnet is better suited for everyday tasks, though it may be a stretch to call mouse brain surgery a common chore. (Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.)
Frontier labs have been planning for more widespread physical manifestations of AI, and researchers have already begun enlisting agents to do other things in the physic
news.summary: An AI agent was used to perform a brain injection on a live mouse, demonstrating how AI can directly control laboratory equipment. The experiment involved an Anthropic model guiding a robotic arm to inject a therapy into the mouse’s brain.
news.enterprise_use: Check your organization’s policies on AI integration with physical equipment—ensure that any automated lab systems have strict access controls and audit logs. Inaction may expose you to unverified AI behaviors that could compromise experimental integrity or safety.

news.title: Spooky New Infostealer Malware Uses AI to ‘Autodox’ Victims
news.summary_raw: Named “Volta-Autodoxer,” the recently uncovered malware uses AI tools to collect troves of data about victims, from login credentials and credit card numbers to Discord sessions and UberEats receipts.
news.source_text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
New research shared exclusively with Kernel Panic shows that hackers have started adding AI functionality into a new strain of infostealer malware, making it possible for the system to automatically profile victims and quickly surface the highest value targets and their information. Dubbed “Volta-Autodoxer” because of how the malware refers to itself internally, the finding by Cisco Talos researchers sheds light on the ways that commercial LLMs are being used to augment and enhance the capabilities of established types of malware.
Often hidden in counterfeit software, infostealers are designed to live up to their name, grabbing usernames, passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, credit card data, and more from infected machines. Many of the biggest data breaches in recent years—from the widespread Snowflake-linked breaches that included AT&T and Ticketmaster to the theft of a terabyte of Disney data—have resulted from hackers accessing targets using login details gathered by infostealers. Overall, the malware has been used to steal hundreds of millions of credentials in recent years.
“Volta is pretty mature as a stealer. It casts a pretty wide net for what it collects,” says Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco Talos. “It compiles all of those things together, ultimately producing a serialized dossier that it can send to a couple LLM models. It’s asking the model to act like an intelligence analyst and produce structured citation-backed assessment of the victim. It’s like a prioritization and analysis function.”
Talos flagged the malware using its new CAIRN framework, built to identify hacking tools that incorporate AI capabilities. Fetterman notes that Talos did not track whether Volta has been used in the wild.
Volta’s traditional infostealer capabilities are powerful and seem to be geared toward targeting younger internet users with robust digital lives. It sweeps for passwords stored in browsers, Microsoft OAuth tokens, cookies, payment cards, and crypto wallet seed phrases, but also active Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions. Then the malware does a second, deeper sweep using its first-round findings. By looking through the target’s Gmail or another central account, Volta builds a fuller picture of the victim, their location, and their habits using data like receipts and order history from services including UberEats and DoorDash.
Once all of this is done, the malware feeds its findings into AI tools for analysis using OpenRouter, a service that can send prompts to multiple different AI providers. Volta defaults its requests to Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6. But apparently preparing for the possibility that the model’s guardrails could block the activity, Volta is built with fallbacks to the Chinese open weight Moonshot
news.summary: Cisco Talos has identified a new AI‑enhanced infostealer called Volta‑Autodoxer that automatically profiles victims and prioritizes credential theft using large language models. The malware can harvest tokens, passwords, and personal data, then feed the findings to LLMs for rapid analysis, raising the threat level for enterprise security stacks.
news.enterprise_use: Go to your endpoint protection console this week and enable AI‑behavior anomaly detection or review existing rules that flag unusual credential exfiltration patterns. Failing to do so may expose your users to automated credential harvesting that bypasses manual rule‑based detection, especially in SSO and MDM environments. The most affected tools are your MDM (JumpCloud), SSO (Okta/JumpCloud), and endpoint security (CrowdStrike, Microsoft Defender) configurations.

news.title: Zest’s new AI agent finds restaurants and books reservations over text
news.summary_raw: Can't agree on where to eat? Zest's AI concierge can combine everyone's tastes, put restaurant options to a vote, and make the reservation.
news.source_text:
Zest, the restaurant discovery app that launched earlier this year, is already thinking about a future where mobile apps are no longer the primary interface. On Thursday, the startup introduced a new feature: a personal AI-powered “restaurant concierge” that lives in your text messages, similar to other popular AI agents like Instinct or Poke.
The launch reflects a broader shift in how startups are thinking about AI, as conversational AI agents take on tasks that had previously required users to launch stand-alone mobile apps. For Zest, that means bringing its restaurant recommendations into texts, then allowing users to immediately take the next step of booking a table.
“The agent is the product now,” explains Zest founder and CEO Mario Gomez-Hall. “You text it, and it answers from your own history and your friends’. It doesn’t need weeks of conversation to learn you because it starts from where you’ve actually been,” he said.
Originally founded in November 2024, with $1.8 million in pre-seed backing from Alexis Ohanian at 776 and Steve Jang at Kindred Ventures, the app’s unique feature is that it links up with users’ credit cards to track where they’re actually eating out to get a sense of their tastes and interests. With this data on hand, Zest can make tailored suggestions of what places you might like to try next, whether that’s in your own city or suggestions of places to try when you’re traveling.
The credit card data used by Zest’s app is imported via the financial services company Plaid, which is used by banks and other fintech and budgeting apps. Zest says it focuses only on those transactions in the food and drink categories when making its personalized map and lists.
The startup’s latest idea is to tackle the same problem — where should I go to eat? — from a new angle. It will now make its suggestions from inside a text message thread and can turn to AI to do things like check availability and make the reservation for you through connected services like OpenTable, Resy, and SevenRooms.
To work, users will text the Zest concierge at (212) 470-6067. What’s even better is that Zest can be dropped into a group chat, where it can blend everyone’s tastes to find places the whole group will love. Here, it can also settle indecision with an in-thread voting feature and then can book a table for the group without leaving the conversation.
Users can ask Zest for recommendations based on a number of factors, like cuisine, craving, occasion, dietary restrictions, or neighborhood, and can ask questions about the restaurants, like how busy the place may be, or whether it offers Wi-Fi, and more. Plus, you can ask Zest to send you the menu to help you make a decision.
In TechCrunch’s tests, the AI worked fairly well, offering a list of suggestions for new places matched to our tastes that also fit particular conditions, like time of day, party size, location, and other factors. While finding an open table is something other apps have offered for year
news.summary: Zest launched an AI‑powered text‑based restaurant concierge that pulls credit‑card data via Plaid to recommend and book tables through OpenTable, Resy, and SevenRooms. The agent operates entirely through SMS, enabling instant reservations without a mobile app.
news.enterprise_use: Check how your organization’s SMS and data privacy policies align with a service that reads credit‑card history; ensure compliance before integrating similar conversational agents. Monitor Plaid’s API usage limits and data handling to mitigate potential security risks in your environment.

news.source_text:
2024-01-14
We have seen in a previous post that switch statements are more complex than they seem. The compiler is able to implement them as a decision tree (even though maybe it shouldn't). Is that everything it can do?
In this post, I'll focus on gcc. All optimizations, except the bitset lowering, translate to clang. I'll be using the -O3 optimization flag unless indicated otherwise.
I've also slightly edited gcc code and removed certain assertions for brevity. 
Let us start with a simple example. 
A function that takes two integers x and val. Depending on the value of x, it calls a corresponding function (f0, f1, and so forth) with val as an argument and returns the result.
Were we to implement this manually, we'd would use an array of function pointers, where the input serves as the index into the array.
int ;
int ;
int ;
int ;
int ;
int 
compact:
	mov	eax, edi
	mov	edi, esi
	cmp	eax, 4
	ja	.L2
	jmp	[QWORD PTR .L4[0+rax*8]]
.L4:
	.quad	.L8
	.quad	.L7
	.quad	.L6
	.quad	.L5
	.quad	.L3
.L5:
	jmp	f3
.L3:
	jmp	f4
.L8:
	jmp	f0
.L7:
	jmp	f1
.L6:
	jmp	f2
.L2:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret
The compiler agrees with this approach, and transforms the switch statement into a jump table.
Moreover, it is able to identify when the values are offset by a constant:

int ;
int ;
int ;
int ;
int 
compact:
	lea	eax, [rdi-97]
	cmp	eax, 4
	ja	.L2
	mov	edi, esi
	jmp	[QWORD PTR .L4[0+rax*8]]
.L4:
	.quad	.L8
	.quad	.L7
	.quad	.L6
	.quad	.L5
	.quad	.L3
.L5:
	jmp	f3
.L3:
	jmp	f4
.L8:
	jmp	f0
.L7:
	jmp	f1
.L6:
	jmp	f2
.L2:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret
Our intuition suggests that the more sparse the values, the less advantageous the jump table conversion is.
Through experimentation, we find that gcc considers the threshold to be around eight jump table entries per case label.
In other words, the following function compiles to a jump table:

	mov	edi, esi
	cmp	eax, 34
	ja	.L2
	jmp	[QWORD PTR .L4[0+rax*8]]
.L4:
	.quad	.L8
	.quad	.L2
	; ...
	.quad	.L2
	.quad	.L7
	.quad	.L2
	; ...
	.quad	.L2
	.quad	.L6
	.quad	.L2
	; ...
	.quad	.L2
	.quad	.L5
	.quad	.L2
	; ...
	.quad	.L2
	.quad	.L3
.L2:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret
.L8:
	jmp	f0
.L7:
	jmp	f1
.L6:
	jmp	f2
.L5:

.L3:
	jmp	f4
But this other function is expanded as a tree of comparisons:

int ;

sparse_8:
	mov	eax, edi
	mov	edi, esi
	cmp	eax, 16
	je	.L2
	jle	.L10
	cmp	eax, 24
	je	.L7
	cmp	eax, 40
	jne	.L1
	jmp	f4
.L10:
	test	eax, eax
	je	.L4
	cmp	eax, 8
	jne	.L1
	jmp	f1
.L1:
	xor	eax, eax
	ret
.L4:
	jmp	f0
.L7:
	jmp	f3
.L2:
	jmp	f2

news.title: Community safety report and new protections for teens
news.summary_raw: OpenAI is strengthening violence prevention in ChatGPT with expanded safeguards, earlier interventions, and a new commitment to public safety reporting.
news.source_text:
Community safety report and new protections for teens
ChatGPT is one of the world’s most widely used AI products, and we have invested in building some of the industry’s most advanced systems for detecting potential harm, reviewing concerning activity, and escalating credible threats. We’re making two announcements to further our work in this area: a new Community Safeguards Report and more restrictions around firearms content for minors.
Keeping communities safe continues to be a top priority for OpenAI. Our work includes bringing imminent threats of violence to the attention of law enforcement, and we made over 200 law enforcement referrals in Q3 2026. These referrals are making a positive(opens in a new window) difference(opens in a new window) in disrupting violent plots, and we continue to rely on mental health and behavioral experts to help us assess difficult cases.
We recognize AI companies have a distinct role to play alongside law enforcement, family members, mental-health professionals, and policymakers, who bring critical authority, context and real-world reach. We are committed to making the most of that role by continuously strengthening our systems, sharing what we learn, and working directly with those who are best positioned to act in the real world.
We are constantly strengthening the steps we take to help protect people and communities. That means building strong safeguards, and also being transparent about how well they work and what we’re doing to enhance them. We want to give people a clear picture of our approach, how our models identify and respond to harmful behavior, the risks we see in practice, and the steps we take to address them.
We’re committing to launch the Community Safety Report on violence prevention and other community safety issues, and the effectiveness of our safeguards. The report will explain how we train our systems to detect, investigate, and respond to community safety issues. We’ll share anonymized examples of how violence-related harm manifests and what we’re learning, highlight new mitigations and policy changes, and include relevant data to support these findings.
We will publish our first report in early 2027, covering the second half of 2026, with updates every six months thereafter. Our commitment is to share meaningful findings about how we identify, review, and respond to potentially harmful content.
Our models are trained to not give instructions that would help someone plan or carry out violence. We’re now placing additional restrictions on how ChatGPT responds to questions about past mass attacks and the people who carried them out, directing the model to provide less detailed information in those areas even if it is available from other online sources. news.summary_raw:

Points: 144
# Comments: 78
news.source_text:
HackerTube
It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with: hackertube.org!
Opus downloaded all comments of HackerNews, filtered them down, ran Sonnet over them in a workflow, got rid of spam and low grade content, and narrowed them down to just 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila!
HackerTube:
- Contains quality content
- Uses the 50% thumbnail instead of the uploaded thumbnail
- Custom and good ForYou recommendations without any user accounts, storing state in local browser session
- Keyboard shortcuts
- Export of the site's data available to give to your agent to easily create your own version
This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5 <3.
news.summary: Opus 5.5 automated the creation of a YouTube clone, HackerTube, by harvesting recommended videos from Hacker News. The resulting site offers quality content and a customized recommendation engine without user accounts.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on HackerTube as a potential benchmark for content recommendation systems; it demonstrates how AI can curate high-quality content efficiently. If your IT team evaluates new content delivery solutions, consider testing HackerTube’s architecture for inspiration. This could inform future internal knowledge bases or intranet media portals.

news.source_text:
GPT-5.6 Sol can beat Factorio
Edit: Woah, this took off! If you want more details you can subscribe at the bottom of the post or on YouTube. I’m working on a more detailed highlights/commentary post and video.
Previously: We got Claude Code playing Factorio, Towards beating Factorio autonomously, and Faketorio: an agent testbed
I got GPT-5.6 Sol, running in Codex with low thinking level, to complete a peaceful (i.e. no biters) Factorio run in 13.5 hours of game time:
A timelapse of the full run is available on YouTube.
Similar to my previous post, this run used a game manager to allow Sol/Codex to interact with the game via a small library (though in this run it was Python rather than Bash). The library allows the model to play the game programmatically while enforcing the same restrictions that human players face when using the GUI (e.g. reach of the player, fog of war).
Observing the run was fascinating: Sol exceeded my expectations in some areas while also showing clear weaknesses in others. I have the entire run recorded and am working on a commentary video, but in the meantime here’s a small timelapsed segment showing some parts of the factory:
Besides the screencast, my run manager also captured production statistics throughout the game. Here’s a chart of total resource production, annotated with science research milestones:
I had planned to terminate the run after blue science research, but Sol’s surprising effectiveness convinced me to keep it going. Unfortunately, the scaling issues I thought would occur in the blue science stage appeared later and slowed Sol’s relative progress significantly.
The rocket launch was only achieved through significant ‘manual’ effort on Sol’s part as it papered over its late-game failures to connect certain production systems by repeatedly ferrying supplies between areas of the factory.
Still, I was pleased with the improvement over previous attempts with GPT-5.5 which suffered from the model’s failures to use transport belts at all.
I’m optimistic about autonomous Factorio play as a medium for building intuition about the nature of model capabilities. In many ways playing Factorio is analogous to programming but with the benefit of being much more legible to casual observers, making it convenient for grounding discussion of model behaviors.
I look forward to testing other models and thinking levels, as well as non-peaceful runs. Stay tuned!
news.summary: OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol has demonstrated autonomous gameplay in Factorio, completing a peaceful run in 13.5 hours. The post showcases the model’s improved strategic planning and highlights ongoing research into AI capabilities.
